newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Columbia sees firmer plan in 90-100 days.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Columbia sees firmer plan in 90-100 days.

text.p: Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp expects to work out a more definitive action plan for changing the company within about 90 to 100 days, said president Jack Bovender on Thursday.
In an interview with Reuters, Bovender said a broad outline of reforms unveiled Thursday was presented to the U.S Justice Department by Columbia attorneys on Wednesday.

"Our lawyers did meet with the Justice Department yesterday, but it was not the intent to ask them to approve or disapprove this outline ... This is our plan and we wanted them to look at it," he said.
"Now what we're hopeful we can do is within the next ... 90 to 100 days come out with a more definitive plan," he said.

As part of a reform plan devised by Bovender and new chief executive Dr. Thomas Frist, Columbia said it will sell its home health business, which consists of 570 locations in 30 states. Its biggest home health markets are Florida, Texas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Georgia, Louisana and Oklahoma. "I'm sure it's going to take months to do this," Bovender said.

Home health has been one of Columbia's fastest-growing businesses, but constitutes less than five percent of revenues. Bovender said he could not say whether or how much the company might have to charge against earnings on the sale.
"I have no idea what the valuation of these are going to be ... We have not looked at that issue at all, but obviously we will be doing that as time goes on," he said.

As the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company, Columbia has been a leader in moving into home health with the strategy of continuing to make money off patients, even after they are discharged from one of its 342 acute-care hospitals.
Owning the home health locations that look after patients sent home from Columbia hospitals may not be necessary to preserve the company's revenue stream in this area, he said.

"What we would like to do is find a strategic partner or strategic partners in market areas that we can spin it off to or spin parts of it off to ... to make sure that we don't lose this continuum of care," Bovender said.

In dealing with the massive federal investigation that has forced a crisis at the Nashville, Tenn.-based hospital giant, Bovender said the next step is for executives to begin meeting with newly hired lawyers and accountants to hash out details of the broad action plan.

Columbia has hired the accounting firm of Deloitte & Touche and the Washington, D.C.-based law firm of Latham & Watkins for help. "I'm sure they will divide their people into teams to work on specific points," Bovender said.

He said he did not know when Columbia executives would be drawn into the meetings with the government, but suggested it could be soon. "I'm sure we're going to be having meetings going forward," he said.

Bovender said he was uncertain how many of its 285,000 employees would be affected by a halt in annual cash incentive pay announced Thursday, but he said most of the impact would be felt in the executive ranks.
"That's where the bulk of it is," he said.

Columbia will not only stop selling equity interests in its hospitals to physicians, it will also attempt to unwind all existing physician syndication deals made over the past nine years, Bovender said.

"We have physician syndications in about 40 of our markets, I believe, involving maybe 100 hospitals. But that only involved about four percent of our total medical staff members across the company," he said.
He said the company will unwind "as many as we can possibly do," he said.
Shares in the company were up 1/2 to 35 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
((--Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8787))
